Experience areas and supervisor roles. Relevant when planning staff development for licensure candidates.

questions.stem:
XYZ Architects is a 30-person firm known for office and laboratory work. Over the past year it hired two staff and lost one. Before committing to two new hospital commissions, the partners review the following data:

| Role | Utilization | Weekly overtime |
|---|---|---|
| Principals | 45% | None |
| Project managers | 78% | Minimal |
| Project architects | 92% | About 6 hours each |
| Designers | 95% | About 6 hours each |

- Backlog is nine months and growing.
- The hospital projects start in three months and will run about two years.
- Both projects require experience with healthcare regulations.
- Cash reserves are healthy, and the line of credit is unused.

Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Engage contract staff for six months, then reassess.
options.explanation: Contract staff suit short peaks. This need lasts about two years and calls for healthcare expertise that temporary production staff rarely bring.

options.text: Hire two permanent project architects with healthcare experience.
options.explanation: Correct. Production staff are already overloaded, the new workload is long-term and specialized, and the firm can afford permanent hires.

options.text: Shift principals onto production work to raise their utilization.
options.explanation: Principals' non-billable time supports leadership, business development and quality review. Moving them to production adds no healthcare expertise.

options.text: Continue the current overtime until the hospital projects begin.
options.explanation: Production staff are already working sustained overtime. Adding two years of work on top invites burnout and errors.

questions.explanation: Match the resource to the duration and nature of the need. A long-term, specialized workload with healthy cash calls for permanent hires with the right experience.

questions.stem:
A 25-person firm has two K-8 school projects whose construction document deadlines are fixed by the district's bond sale schedule. The partners estimate that production needs will run about 30% above current capacity for the next four months, then return to normal as both projects move into bidding. Cash reserves are modest, and two qualified drafters are available through a local staffing agency.

Which staffing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Hire four permanent production staff.
options.explanation: Permanent hires would leave the firm overstaffed, and carrying their salaries, once the four-month peak ends.

options.text: Engage contract staff for the four-month peak.
options.explanation: Correct. Contract staff add capacity only for as long as it's needed, without long-term salary and benefit commitments.

options.text: Ask the district to move the bid dates.
options.explanation: The bid dates are tied to the bond sale. Asking to move them shifts the firm's capacity problem onto the client.

options.text: Outsource the complete document set for one school.
options.explanation: Handing off an entire set weakens the firm's control over documents it must seal. Outsourcing fits discrete tasks better.

questions.explanation: Short, defined peaks → flexible capacity. Sustained growth → permanent staff.

questions.stem:
A 40-person firm has designed office buildings for 20 years. Its strategic plan calls for entering the outpatient healthcare market, and a long-time client has asked it to design a 20,000 sf clinic next year. No one on staff has completed a healthcare project, but the firm has strong BIM capabilities and a well-established quality-control program.

Which initial step best positions the firm to deliver the clinic competently?

options.text: Purchase healthcare planning software for the design team.
options.explanation: Tools don't provide the regulatory and clinical-planning knowledge healthcare projects require.

options.text: Team with an experienced healthcare firm initially.
options.explanation: Correct. Teaming brings proven expertise right away and shares risk while the firm's staff gain experience (NCARB Rule 1.3).

options.text: Assign the firm's strongest designer to lead the first clinic.
options.explanation: Design talent in another building type isn't healthcare expertise.

options.text: Rely on the firm's quality-control program to catch gaps.
options.explanation: QC checks documents against what the firm knows. It can't supply healthcare knowledge the firm lacks.

questions.explanation: Practice only where you, together with those you engage, have the needed knowledge and skill.

questions.stem:
A firm is evaluating a reality-capture system for its renovation practice. The partners have gathered the following:

- Equipment and software: $36,000
- Initial staff training: $6,000
- Annual software subscription: $3,000
- Expected annual savings in field-survey labor: $15,000
- Expected annual profit from new renovation work: $9,000

Based on total cost of ownership, what is the simple payback period?

options.text: 1.50 years
options.explanation: This leaves out both the training cost and the annual subscription ($36,000 ÷ $24,000).

options.text: 1.71 years
options.explanation: This leaves out the training cost ($36,000 ÷ $21,000).

options.text: 1.75 years
options.explanation: This leaves out the annual subscription ($42,000 ÷ $24,000).

options.text: 2.00 years

questions.stem:
A firm's 10-person production studio has worked at 92% utilization for two quarters, and overtime keeps climbing. Firm policy targets 80% utilization for production staff, leaving time for training and quality reviews. The partners expect the studio's chargeable workload to stay at its current level for at least two years.

| Studio data | Value |
|---|---|
| Production staff | 10 |
| Hours per person per year | 2,080 |
| Current utilization | 92% |
| Target utilization | 80% |

How many additional production staff does the studio need to meet the target at the current workload?

options.explanation: This multiplies 10 staff by the 12-point gap and rounds down, ignoring that each new hire is also limited to 80%.
Correct. The workload needs 11.5 people at 80%, which rounds up to 12, so the studio needs 2 more.
That's the total staff needed, not the number of additional hires.

questions.explanation:
1. Chargeable hours = 10 × 2,080 × 0.92 = 19,136
2. Chargeable hours per person at target = 2,080 × 0.80 = 1,664
3. Staff needed = 19,136 ÷ 1,664 = 11.5, rounded up to 12
4. Additional staff = 12 − 10 = 2

questions.stem:
Over two quarters, firm-wide utilization at a 40-person firm has risen from 76% to 91%. Overtime has doubled, two project architects have resigned, and the remaining project architects say they no longer have time to mentor junior staff. Backlog has stayed steady at about six months, and fees on current projects are on budget.

What should management do first?

options.text: Raise billing rates to moderate incoming work.
options.explanation: Rate changes may be warranted later, but they don't address the current overload or its cause.

options.text: Compare staffing levels with the projected workload.
options.explanation: Correct. The data point to under-staffing. Quantifying the gap between capacity and workload is the first step toward hiring or rebalancing.

options.text: Reduce time allocated to marketing and training.
options.explanation: Cutting non-billable time raises utilization further and harms the future pipeline. It deepens the problem.

options.text: Offer retention bonuses to the remaining project architects.
options.explanation: Bonuses may help retention, but they treat a symptom without fixing the workload that's driving resignations.

questions.explanation: High and rising utilization, overtime and turnover together signal overload. Diagnose capacity before acting.

questions.stem:
A 60-person firm has had three former employees challenge their terminations in the past two years. Each time, the firm had little written record of performance concerns. The principals are redesigning the annual performance review process so it supports staff development and holds up if a personnel decision is challenged.

Which practices should the new process include?

options.text: Measure performance against expectations set at the start of the period
options.explanation: Correct. Pre-set expectations make the review fair and measurable.

options.text: Document each review and the agreed development goals
options.explanation: Correct. Written records support development plans and personnel decisions.

options.text: Base ratings primarily on each employee's utilization rate
options.explanation: Utilization is one input. It ignores quality, leadership and growth.

options.text: Hold reviews only when performance concerns arise
options.explanation: Problem-only reviews feel punitive and miss development opportunities.

options.text: Use identical goals for every employee regardless of role
options.explanation: Goals should reflect each role's responsibilities and the employee's development path.

options.text: Let project managers set each employee's salary increase
options.explanation: Compensation decisions need consistent firm-wide criteria, not project-by-project judgment.

questions.explanation: Effective reviews are regular, criteria-based, documented and development-focused.

questions.stem:
A 12-person firm relies on one senior architect for all specification writing and code reviews. She has been with the firm 15 years, has given no sign of leaving, and is the only person who knows the firm's master specification system. The principals worry about what would happen if she were unavailable for an extended period during a busy year.

Which action most directly reduces the firm's risk?

options.text: Provide the architect with a retention bonus.
options.explanation: A bonus may delay a departure, but the firm still depends on one person's knowledge.

options.text: Document her procedures and cross-train two staff members.
options.explanation: Correct. Spreading the knowledge reduces key-person risk no matter what happens to the individual.

options.text: Outsource specification writing to a specifications consultant.
options.explanation: This moves the dependency to an outside party, and code reviews still rest on one person.

options.text: Purchase key-person insurance on the architect.
options.explanation: Insurance pays money if she dies. It doesn't preserve the knowledge or cover a resignation or disability.

questions.explanation: Key-person risk is reduced by spreading knowledge: documentation, cross-training, succession planning.

questions.stem:
A 35-person firm reviews staffing quarterly. Over the next quarter, six of its projects will move from construction documents into construction. Each CD team includes designers, production staff and a project architect, and most of each project's remaining fee is in the construction phase. Two staff members with extensive construction administration experience are finishing assignments on other projects.

Which staffing adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Shift the experienced CA staff onto those projects.
options.explanation: Correct. Submittal review, RFIs, site observation and pay applications call for contract-administration skills, and the remaining fee supports a smaller, specialized team.

options.text: Keep each full design team intact through construction.
options.explanation: Continuity of a project lead helps, but full design teams would overspend the smaller construction-phase fee.

options.text: Assign submittal review to each project's designers.
options.explanation: Submittal review is a technical, contract-administration task. Designers may lack the construction experience it needs.

options.text: Assign construction administration to junior staff to conserve fee.
options.explanation: CA involves contractual judgment and liability. Junior staff need supervision, not sole responsibility.

questions.explanation: Staffing should change with each project phase, matching both the skills needed and the fee available.

questions.stem:
The partners of a 20-person firm adopted a strategic plan calling for energy-performance consulting for existing clients within two years. The firm has no energy-modeling capability today, two staff members have offered to lead the new service, and the year's capital budget is limited.

Which investments best support this goal?

options.text: Energy-modeling software with training for a core group
options.explanation: Correct. Tools plus trained people create a deliverable capability.

options.text: Sustainability credentials and continuing education for staff
options.explanation: Correct. Expertise and recognized credentials build competence and credibility in the new service.

options.text: A larger office to accommodate future growth
options.explanation: Adding overhead ahead of revenue doesn't build the needed capability.

options.text: High-capacity plotters for faster document production
options.explanation: Production equipment doesn't advance energy-performance services.

options.text: Expanded marketing of the firm's existing services
options.explanation: Marketing current services doesn't develop the new capability.

options.text: Rendering workstation upgrades for design staff
options.explanation: Visualization hardware isn't central to energy-performance analysis.

questions.explanation: Capital spending should map directly to strategic goals.

questions.stem:
A profitable firm needs eight high-performance workstations now for current BIM projects. Several large clients have been paying slowly, and cash on hand is tight. The vendor offers two options:

- Purchase: $36,000 now, plus $2,000 per year for maintenance
- Lease: $1,250 per month for 36 months, maintenance included

Considering the three-year cost and the firm's situation, which choice is most appropriate?

options.text: Lease; it costs $3,000 more but preserves cash.
options.explanation: Correct. Leasing costs $45,000 versus $42,000 to buy, but it keeps scarce cash available while receivables are slow.

options.text: Purchase; it saves $3,000 over three years.
options.explanation: The math is right, but spending $36,000 up front drains the cash the firm needs now.

options.text: Purchase; it saves $9,000 over three years.
options.explanation: This leaves out the $6,000 of maintenance that comes with purchasing.

options.text: Lease; it costs $3,000 less over the three years.
options.explanation: Leasing costs $3,000 more, not less.

questions.explanation:
1. Purchase = $36,000 + (3 × $2,000) = $42,000
2. Lease = 36 × $1,250 = $45,000
3. Lease costs $3,000 more, but a cash constraint favors leasing for a profitable, cash-poor firm.

flashcards.back: Contracted work not yet earned. Compare it with staff capacity to forecast staffing needs.
Chargeable (billable) hours ÷ total hours. Too high signals overload; too low signals idle capacity.

flashcards.front: Best response to a short-term workload peak
flashcards.back: Flexible capacity: contract staff, limited overtime, or outsourcing a discrete task, not permanent hires.

flashcards.front: Best response to sustained growth or a new service line
flashcards.back: Permanent hires (or partners) with the right skills, supported by training.

flashcards.front: Total cost of ownership for technology
flashcards.back: Purchase or subscription + implementation + training + productivity loss while learning + ongoing support and upgrades.
Investment ÷ annual net benefit (savings + added profit).

flashcards.front: Lease vs. buy: when to lease
flashcards.back: When cash is tight or the technology turns over quickly. Leasing keeps working capital in the firm and makes upgrades easier.
Cross-training, written procedures and office standards, and succession planning.

flashcards.front: What a defensible staff evaluation needs
flashcards.back: Regular schedule, pre-set written expectations, documentation, and development goals.

flashcards.front: How staffing changes from CDs to construction
flashcards.back: Fewer hours, and shift to people with field, submittal and contract-administration skills.

flashcards.front: Three ingredients for entering a new practice area
flashcards.back: Experienced people (hire or partner), training or credentials, and the right tools, together.

flashcards.front: Why very high utilization is a warning sign
flashcards.back: No time left for marketing, training or QC; predicts overtime, burnout and turnover.
